supporting_evidence.summary: significant deviations in scope [all services]: recommendationservice_latency-90 z=2400.08 (12000.4%); recommendationservice_latency-50 z=178.29 (891.5%); frontend_latency-90 z=53.27 (286.5%); recommendationservice_cpu z=52.79 (620.8%)
traces for recommendationservice: SIGNIFICANT change; own spans self-time p50 0.96->2.92ms (3.03x), errors 0.0->0.0; inbound calls self-time p50 3.79->57.01ms (15.04x), errors 0.0->0.0

alternatives_rejected.candidate: frontend: upstream victim of recommendationservice slowness
alternatives_rejected.why: frontend latency-90 deviation (z=53.27) is tiny next to recommendationservice latency-90 (z=2400.08), per E1. E2 shows calls into recommendationservice slowed 15x, so frontend is waiting on it, not causing it.

A pure network delay would not drive CPU up 620.8% (z=52.79, E1). E2 also shows the service's own span self-time grew 3x, meaning the slowdown is inside the process, consistent with CPU contention plus request queueing.

proposed_fix.description: Find and stop the CPU hog in the recommendationservice pod (check for a runaway process or stress workload). Meanwhile, scale out recommendationservice replicas and/or raise its CPU limit. Then verify that recommendationservice and frontend p90 latency return to baseline.

investigation.thought: No evidence yet, so the first step is an unfiltered metric_query that ranks every service and metric by deviation and shows where to look.

Metrics single out recommendationservice: its p90 latency is up about 120x and its CPU is up too. A second telemetry kind is needed, so caller-observed traces should show whether recommendationservice itself is slow or only a victim.

Metrics (E1) and traces (E2) both independently point at recommendationservice: it has the largest latency deviation by far, and its CPU rose sharply (z=52.79, +620.8%), which fits CPU saturation better than injected network delay.
